COP31: the Antalya summit ends without a deal as the EU rejects a text that doesn't even mention fossil fuels, a first since 2009

On Sunday, November 22, after 44 hours of overtime, Turkey's COP31 presidency acknowledged that no agreement was possible. The European Union, the United Kingdom, Norway, Panama and island states rejected a text that was silent on coal, oil and gas but supportive of carbon capture [1][5][6].

At the closing session, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey's minister, announced that the proposed decisions had not been adopted and that no new draft would be presented [1][3]. It is the first time since 2009 that a UN climate conference has ended without an agreement [6].
The final draft mentioned neither coal, oil nor gas, and did not repeat the Dubai (2023) commitment to transition away from fossil fuels; it did, however, call for electrification [6][7].
The text set a target of capturing at least 500 million tonnes of industrial CO2 per year by 2035, wording its critics saw as a license to keep pumping oil [5][6].

On adaptation, the numerical target of $120 billion a year for poor countries had disappeared from the revised version: all that remained was a call to "at least triple" this funding by 2035, with no baseline year [6]. With the text rejected, these commitments fall away [6].

According to Reuters, Saudi Arabia did not budge: no mention of fossil fuels, and carbon capture in the text. Speaking for the Arab League, Riyadh denied any greenwashing [5]. Russia rejected "any wording" on fossil fuels [6].
China and India accepted the text [5][6]. EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra called it "not acceptable" and had warned that "no deal is better than a bad deal" [3][10].
A few procedural decisions survive, such as the work program on climate finance adopted at the opening on November 9 [6][8]. The next formal negotiation will take place at COP32 next year [6].
Key takeaway: for the first time since Copenhagen in 2009, nearly 200 countries are leaving without a common text, and the Dubai pledge to transition away from fossil fuels was not repeated [6][7].

The standoff is clear: on one side, the EU and about 130 countries that called in a letter for fossil fuels to be mentioned [10]; on the other, oil producers led by Riyadh, who are betting on carbon capture [5]. Murat Kurum urged delegates not to "get stuck on one word" [3].

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was "deeply disappointed" and recalled that there is "no ambiguity in the science" [4]. Former US Vice President Al Gore denounced a "veto" by a handful of petro-states [7].
For poor countries, the failure has a concrete cost: the tripling of adaptation funding decided in Belém in 2025, about $120 billion by 2035, still has no roadmap [6].

Nothing changes right away for you: France's and the EU's climate targets are set by their own laws. But without a global framework, Europe moves forward more on its own, which revives the debate over the cost of its transition and energy prices.

Four days after the Shenzhen summit, Beijing vows to retaliate against the United States for cutting its three telecom giants off from US phone numbers

China's Commerce Ministry demanded on Sunday, November 22 that Washington "immediately" reverse the decision by the US telecom regulator (FCC) barring China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from obtaining US phone numbers directly. Beijing calls it "malicious" and vows to defend its interests [1][2][3].
On November 19, the FCC voted to bar China Mobile, China Telecom, China Unicom and other internet telephony (VoIP) providers from "direct access" to US numbers [4][5].

Direct access lets companies obtain numbers without going through an intermediary carrier: it is cheaper and provides advanced calling features. From now on, new national security checks will be required to obtain it [4][5].

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr presents the measure as the "first line of defense against bad actors and illegal robocalls", those often fraudulent automated calls [5]. The FCC considers the three groups' US operations "vulnerable to exploitation and influence" by the Chinese government [4].
The vote took place a few hours after the meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit [3].

On Sunday, China's Commerce Ministry accused the FCC of "overstretching" the concept of national security and of making accusations "with no factual basis". In its view, the measure violates the principles of non-discrimination and fair competition [1][2][6].

Beijing also argues that it runs counter to the "important consensus" reached by the two heads of state. It is calling for a return to negotiations and vows to take the "necessary measures" to protect its interests [1][6].
Finally, the ministry warns that these decisions risk further separating the two countries' telecom industries. The sources do not say how many numbers are affected [6].
Key takeaway: despite the smiles in Shenzhen, the tech rivalry between Washington and Beijing goes on, and every new measure triggers a response [1][3].

The FCC had already barred the three Chinese state-owned carriers from providing international telecom services in the United States [6]. US regulators are also considering revoking direct-access authorizations already granted to companies deemed risky [5].

Washington cites the fight against fraud and national security; Beijing sees it as a disguised sanction against its companies [1][4]. Some media note that the FCC has not published evidence that these carriers were used for robocalls [5].
The timing matters: Beijing points out that this vote came right after a meeting meant to ease relations [1][3]. It remains to be seen what form Beijing's promised retaliation will take [1].

Nothing changes in your daily life. But this battle shows that telecoms, like chips, have become a weapon between China and the United States. Each move can provoke retaliation, with effects on companies and technology prices.

Lithuania: a few kilometers from Belarus, the German army tests kamikaze drones and AI targeting for the first time

On Sunday, November 22, the Bundeswehr carried out its first tactical trials of loitering munitions, drones that dive onto their target, in Lithuania. Supplied by German start-ups Helsing and Stark, they struck tanks as the head of the army looked on. A German brigade of 5,000 soldiers is due to be stationed there by the end of 2027 [1][2][3].
The trials took place at the Rūdninkai training area, near the border with Belarus, during the "Freedom Shield" exercise [1][3].
Loitering munitions from Helsing and Stark, fitted with inert warheads (no explosives), dove from the sky to hit battle tanks, in the presence of army chief Christian Freuding [1][2].

A few days earlier, German soldiers had tested Helsing's Clarity software for the first time, an artificial intelligence that analyzes data from satellites, drones and sensors to help commanders spot targets and suggest actions [1][3].
These drones are intended for Panzerbrigade 45, the armored brigade Germany is setting up in Lithuania, which is due to receive them in 2027, according to the Defense Ministry [1][3].
Berlin only decided in 2025 to buy this type of weapon, after years of controversy over armed drones [1].
The same day, Finland confirmed that Russian ships were towing out of its waters a Russian cargo ship hit by drones, which had caught fire and drifted into its territorial waters [4].
Key takeaway: Germany, long reluctant to arm drones, is learning the lessons of the war in Ukraine and putting them into practice on NATO's eastern flank, facing Moscow's ally Belarus [1][3].
In 2023, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius pledged to permanently station a combat brigade in Lithuania, a first for Berlin: 5,000 soldiers are due to be deployed there by the end of 2027 [1][2].
The choice of Helsing and Stark, two young defense companies, also shows that European rearmament money no longer goes only to the big established manufacturers [1].

The Baltic region is on edge: Sweden has reinstated controls at its internal Schengen borders from November 12, 2026 to May 11, 2027, citing a heightened threat of Russian sabotage [5]. The Kremlin denies any involvement in hybrid attacks in Europe [5].

Europe's rearmament now relies on cheap drones and AI software, not just tanks and planes. It is a sector where public money is pouring in, in Germany as in France, and it weighs more and more on national budgets.

Kenya-DR Congo: in Oyo, Ruto and Tshisekedi bury the hatchet and will restore their ambassadors after years of estrangement

On Sunday, November 22 in Oyo, Congo-Brazzaville, Kenyan President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Félix Tshisekedi agreed to restore their ambassadors and resume cooperation. The four-way summit also brought together the host, Denis Sassou Nguesso, and Togo's Faure Gnassingbé, the African Union mediator [1][2][3].
The so-called "quadripartite" summit was held in Oyo, in northern Congo-Brazzaville, the home of President Denis Sassou Nguesso; its official agenda had not been published [3][5].

According to the Kenyan press, the two countries will work to restore representation at ambassador level, hold regular political consultations and revive their Joint Permanent Commission for Cooperation [1][2].

The recalled Congolese ambassador is to return to his post in Nairobi, and Kenya's ambassador-designate is to present his credentials in Kinshasa [2]. According to L'Horizon africain, the leaders pledged to "create the conditions" for easing tensions [5].
William Ruto cut short a tour of western Kenya and left the country on Saturday, November 21 via Kisumu airport, without prior announcement [4][6].
Faure Gnassingbé, President of Togo's Council of Ministers, is the mediator appointed by the African Union in the conflict between DR Congo and Rwanda [3].

The crisis dates back to December 15, 2023: that day, in Nairobi, the former head of Congo's electoral commission, Corneille Nangaa, launched the Congo River Alliance (AFC), the political coalition allied with the M23 rebels. Kinshasa recalled its ambassador [1][7].

Since then, DR Congo has twice refused to accredit Kenyan ambassadors, Shem Amadi and then Peter Tum, appointed in March 2025, and in August 2025 objected to the appointment of a Kenyan consul in Goma [7][8].

Key takeaway: Kinshasa is mending ties with Nairobi, which it accused of harboring the M23's political allies, after a rift of nearly three years, at a time when it is seeking support against the rebellion [1][3][7].

Kenya had defended its position in the name of freedom of expression: in Kenya, citizens and foreigners can speak to the media without government interference [7]. Kinshasa saw it as support for rebels who in 2025 seized Goma and Bukavu, the capitals of North and South Kivu [9].

The peace process remains fragile. The Doha framework agreement, negotiated with Qatar, was signed in November 2025, but in early November the FRN coalition, which brings together the M23 and former president Joseph Kabila, threatened to leave the talks if Kinshasa holds a constitutional referendum that could open the way to a third term for Tshisekedi [9].
Not all details of the final communiqué have been published, and nothing yet confirms that the Kenyan ambassador has been accredited [2][5].

Eastern DR Congo, where the M23 is fighting, is rich in minerals used in electronics and batteries. Every step toward calm in the region matters for the stability of these supplies, and therefore for European industry.

New Zealand: still without a new government, Luxon calls Putin a "killer" and breaks with Trump, four days before the official results

Caretaker prime minister since the general election in early November, Christopher Luxon on Monday, November 23 called Vladimir Putin a "killer", a few days after crossing paths with him at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. His right-wing coalition has only a one-seat lead, and the official results are due on November 27 [1][4][5].

Christopher Luxon was reacting to Donald Trump's warm words toward Vladimir Putin. According to him, they were followed almost immediately by a massive Russian missile attack on apartment buildings in Kyiv [1][2].

He is speaking as head of a caretaker government: preliminary results give 42 seats to his National Party, 36 to Labour, 16 to the Greens, 13 to ACT, 12 to NZ First, 7 to the new Opportunity party and 5 to Te Pāti Māori [4].

The outgoing National-ACT-NZ First alliance totals 67 seats out of 131, one more than the 66 needed for a majority. This margin rests on 10 overhang seats and on electorates won by a few hundred votes [4].
About 399,000 special votes remain to be counted; the Electoral Commission will publish the official result on November 27 [4][5].

Luxon says he has spoken to the leaders of ACT, NZ First and Opportunity [5]. David Seymour (ACT) wants a single three-way agreement and is demanding the finance portfolio: Luxon does not have the "moral authority" to keep it within the National Party, he says [6].
According to lawyer Graeme Edgeler, the parties should wait for the official count; a four-way alliance with Opportunity would almost certainly have a majority even if the special votes go badly [4].
Key takeaway: a close US ally is publicly distancing itself from Trump on Russia, while its own political future is not yet secure [1][4].
The election weakened both major parties: for the first time, National and Labour are both below 30% [7]. Luxon should stay in power, but with a weaker hand against his partners [7].
Negotiations look set to be long, with a "fairly frustrating" period ahead, the New Zealand press warned [3]. Opportunity has promised to talk first to the party that came out on top [5].
In the meantime, issues are piling up: asked about the pay equity settlement for teacher aides, Luxon replied that it would be up to the next government to decide on a possible appeal [8].

New Zealand carries little weight in the global economy, but its voice matters in the Western camp. When a US ally openly criticizes Trump's line on Russia, it shows that support for Ukraine also divides Washington's partners.

Uganda: ahead of its first barrel, expected in mid-2027, Kampala hands trader Vitol the sale of its oil for ten years

The Ugandan government has signed a ten-year contract with trader Vitol to sell its "Pearl Sweet" crude abroad, loaded at the Tanzanian port of Tanga at the end of the EACOP pipeline. Signed on Friday, November 20 in Entebbe and made public on Saturday, the deal paves the way for first production expected before the end of June 2027 [1][2][3].
The agreement was signed at State House in Entebbe between Vitol, the national oil company UNOC and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development [1][3].
Vitol will market the crude internationally and seek the best buyers and prices; UNOC keeps control over transactions and the choice of customers [1][2].
The trader will first train UNOC's teams, so that the state company can eventually sell its oil on its own [2][4].

The first sales will be "FOB" at Tanga, Tanzania: the buyer takes the oil at the port, the terminus of the EACOP pipeline. The government may later extend the deal to transport all the way to the destination [1][2].

"They will sell our petroleum products to the highest bidder," President Yoweri Museveni summed up [5]. The deal extends a fuel supply contract signed with Vitol in 2023 and in operation since July 2024 [1].
First production, initially planned for July 2026, has been pushed back to before the end of June 2027: the war in the Middle East delayed the delivery of equipment for the pumping stations [6][7].
The EACOP pipeline, 92% complete, should be able to receive crude around mid-December 2026 [6][7].
Key takeaway: Uganda is securing a global seller for its oil, the first concrete step before becoming an exporting country [1][6].
The volumes are significant for East Africa: the Tilenga field is expected to reach a maximum of 190,000 barrels per day and Kingfisher 40,000, or about 230,000 barrels per day in total [7].
The head of TotalEnergies explained that Kingfisher can only start once the pipeline is "fully commissioned", which makes the timetable dependent on the last pieces of equipment [7].
Choosing "FOB" leaves shipping from Tanga to Vitol and the buyers, but the state keeps the option of later taking over part of the chain, and therefore part of the margin [1][2].

French group TotalEnergies is involved in the project: its CEO himself set the start-up timetable. The launch of this oil in 2027 will matter for its results, and for the European debate on new oil projects.

Stellantis meets its employees this Monday to exit motorsport, Peugeot reportedly leaving Le Mans: on the stock market, the giant is now worth barely more than Renault

Stellantis is holding two extraordinary meetings this Monday, November 23 with employee representatives of its racing subsidiary. According to Le Figaro, the group will stop investing in motorsport: Peugeot would leave endurance racing and the 24 Hours of Le Mans, Citroën and Opel would leave Formula E. On the stock market, Stellantis was worth only €9.54 billion on November 18, barely more than Renault [1][2][5].

According to Le Figaro, cited by Reuters, Stellantis is set to announce an end to its investments in motorsport: Peugeot would leave the World Endurance Championship (WEC), Citroën and Opel would leave Formula E [1].
Lancia, which competes in rallying, would also be affected: according to the US site Jalopnik, the group would leave all its competitions except Nascar in the United States [4].

Stellantis has not commented, but confirmed two extraordinary meetings on Monday with employee representatives of Stellantis Motorsport [1]. A Peugeot spokesperson confirmed these meetings to the site Sportscar365 [2].
If Peugeot leaves, no French manufacturer will be on the WEC grid in 2027, as Alpine has already announced its departure [2].
According to DailySportsCar, the decision comes amid difficult negotiations with unions over job cuts and wages, after heavy losses linked to electric cars [3].

On the stock market, Stellantis was worth €9.54 billion at the close on November 18, compared with €8.12 billion for Renault, even though it sells about three times as many cars, according to ItalPassion [5]. Investir Simplement notes a one-year low of €3.52 per share [6].
CEO Antonio Filosa is trying to turn the group around after two years of falling sales and profitability, Reuters notes [1]. Stellantis is targeting €6 billion in annual savings by 2028 [9].

Key takeaway: motorsport is expensive and mainly brings in image. When a carmaker is losing money, it is one of the first expenses to be cut, because it does not directly affect factories or sales [1][3].

Stellantis is in the middle of a cost-cutting drive. In 2025, the group lost €22.3 billion, due to €25.4 billion in exceptional charges, mostly linked to electric cars [7]. It has suspended its 2026 dividend [8].

The stock market is punishing this track record: the market now values Stellantis barely above Renault, which is three times smaller by volume [5]. For investors, the question is whether savings, such as quitting racing, will be enough to return to profit.
The first signs are mixed: in the third quarter of 2026, adjusted operating income rose to €256 million, compared with €90 million a year earlier, but the group burned about €4 billion in cash [10].

If you own Stellantis shares, or a French equity fund that holds them, quitting motorsport won't change much on its own: sales and cash are what matter. For fans, it probably means the end of Peugeot at Le Mans in 2027.

How it works: stock market value, or "market capitalization"

A company's stock market value, its market capitalization, is the price of one share multiplied by the number of shares. It does not measure a company's size, but what investors think it will earn in the future. Stellantis sells about three times as many cars as Renault, but is now worth only €1.4 billion more on the stock market [5]. Why? Investors look at future profits and risk. After a €22.3 billion loss in 2025 [7] and a suspended dividend [8], they want proof of a turnaround before paying more. Cutting spending such as racing is a signal, but not proof.

Portuguese lawmakers wrap up their detailed review of Luís Montenegro's government's 2027 budget this Monday, November 23, ahead of the final vote on Tuesday the 24th. The minority government depends on the Socialist Party's abstention [1][2][3].

On November 5, it surprised markets by cutting its rate by a quarter point, to 6.25% [3]: another cut would make credit cheaper but could weaken the peso, while a pause would signal that rate cuts are over for a while.
